title: Astros' AL West dominance may face a $4 billion threat in Southern California
description: The Astros' longtime divisional punching bag just gained one of the richest and most accomplished owners in sports.
fullText:
The Houston Astros have essentially owned the American League West for a decade now, winning seven division titles, four American League pennants and two World Series championships. However, the Astros' divisional dominance could be up for grabs, as the organization must manage an aging roster and a likely need for new leadership in multiple positions.

On Tuesday, a new threat entered the proverbial AL West chat, with a resume that features a championship-winning pedigree across every major sport on two continents.

Billionaire team owner Stan Kroenke and Kroenke Sports Entertainment (KSE) entered into a definitive agreement on Tuesday to purchase the Los Angeles Angels from the Arte Moreno family for a reported MLB-record $4 billion. The transaction is expected to close in early 2027.

"The Angels are a storied franchise anchored in a great market," Kroenke said in a statement released by both the Angels and Kroenke Sports & Entertainment. "We look forward to an exciting future with the Angels organization."

Kroenke, who owns four franchises across four leagues, will likely bring a fresh perspective to a franchise that's been moribund and listless. The Angels are on track to miss the postseason for the 12th straight year and have essentially wasted the prime years of two of the best baseball talents of a generation in Shohei Ohtani and Mike Trout.

Under Kroenke's leadership, his teams have all won titles in the past five years, including:

English Premier League's Arsenal, 2026

A championship standard is now attainable KSE's as foundation for success, not just an aspirational one. Josh Kroenke, Arsenal's co-chairman, demonstrated these aspirations when hiring Andrea Berta as the club's new sporting director.

"I went to Andrea, and I laid out our championship rings," Josh Kroenke said to James Benge of CBS in May. "I said: 'This is what we're here for. So as we start to shape our thinking, know this is what we're going for.' He was looking at them pretty close!"

KSE isn't simply purchasing a baseball team; they're buying back into Southern California in an area that's highly valuable yet wholly undeveloped in Orange County. Kroenke's institutional knowledge means there is a real possibility of turning an aging ballpark and sports district into another year-round real estate and entertainment engine.

"The addition of the Angels to the KSE portfolio creates the opportunity for a year-round Southern California calendar of events," reads a statement from KSE on their future strategy.

The Angels sit on land-currently owned by the City of Anaheim-that could ultimately be more valuable than the team itself. Angel Stadium sits on approximately 150 acres, with surrounding areas potentially up for grabs. In fact, KSE recently developed SoFi Stadium as the anchor of a 300-acre Hollywood Park entertainment district focused on retail, offices, residences and hotels.

The Angels' reputation has suffered greatly under previous ownership, as the squandering of talents like Ohtani and Moreno has coincided with reports of downsizing in scouting, development and organizational resources. KSE's ownership has continually focused on stadium upgrades, revamped clubhouses, sports science investment and family-friendly facilities for players.

That type of resource commitment is enough to attract marquee players to any organization, but offering a Southern California lifestyle that includes year-round good weather, access to beaches, major entertainment opportunities, and increased endorsement potential can be a big joker in negotiations.

"Kroenke's got a track record of success and winning championships with his teams," Trout said to reporters on Tuesday. "I'm super excited about it and can't wait to meet him."

Just ask the Los Angeles Dodgers about offering such a benefit to free agents.

The Astros already booted their general manager in August, and Joe Espada's tenure as manager is clearly in doubt. Moreover, Astros owner Jim Crane has already shown hesitancy to spend big, instead relying on a cautious, methodical approach.

That strategy served the Astros well during their title-winning run, as their roster was stacked with future Hall of Famers and a minor league system stocked with future All-Stars. The club also featured rising stars in various leadership positions that proved to be innovative (and at times, too clever) before moving on to other teams. Playing in a warm-weather city with lucrative tax benefits has always been a plus, but for some, playing in Southern California has an appeal all its own.

The AL West includes teams that are either resource-rich but inconsistent, like the Seattle Mariners and Texas Rangers, or struggling significantly, such as the Athletics and Angels. In this environment, being consistently competent has been key to success, as the Astros have demonstrated for over a decade. But 2026 has proven how low the bar is for competency.

"The reality is no AL West team really deserves to reach the postseason this year. All five teams deserve to go home at the end of September," Yahoo MLB insider Russell Dorsey said in August. "But it doesn't work that way in baseball. So we all have to resign ourselves to watching maybe the saddest division race MLB has ever seen."

The Astros have a 138-89 record against the Angels since joining the AL West in 2013, but competency has now landed in Southern California. The Astros should prepare themselves accordingly.

title: Prosecutors Say a North Carolina Teenager Committed Murder by Livestreaming a California Mosque Shooting (opinion)
description: The case smacks of a desire for retribution that cannot be satisfied by prosecuting the actual killers, who committed suicide.
fullText:
A grand jury in Forsyth County, North Carolina, this week indicted a Winston-Salem teenager, Sarah Lindsey Santiago, on three charges of murder in connection with the May 18 shooting at the Islamic Center of San Diego. The perpetrators of that attack, 17-year-old Cain Clark and 18-year-old Caleb Vazquez, killed themselves shortly afterward. Santiago was not present during their crimes, and her alleged participation consisted mainly of helping to livestream the attack and posting the killers' manifesto.

Because Santiago aided and abetted Clark and Vazquez, Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O'Neill said at a press conference on Monday, she is guilty of first-degree murder, which in North Carolina is punishable by a mandatory penalty of life in prison without parole when the defendant is 18 or older. Since Santiago is 17, she could, if convicted, receive a life sentence with the possibility of parole after 25 years based on a claim of "mitigating circumstances."

Assuming the allegations against Santiago are true, her conduct was morally reprehensible and potentially criminal. But the decision to charge her with first-degree murder smacks of a desire for retribution that in this case cannot be satisfied by prosecuting the actual killers. Worse, O'Neill's explanation of that decision mixes the elements of aiding and abetting with concerns about the promotion of bigotry and glorification of violence, even by people with no advance knowledge of any actual crimes.

"My client is innocent of all these charges," said Santiago's lawyer, Alan Doorasamy. The case "touches on major issues in the U.S., including youth and social media and mental health," he added. "The world will soon know the facts that caused this major tragedy."

According to O'Neill, Santiago never met Clark or Vazquez in person but communicated with them online. He said she was aware of their plan to attack the San Diego mosque and knew that they also planned to attack a synagogue and "a predominantly African-American high school." Far from reporting or discouraging those plans, the indictment says, she endorsed them, to the point that she sent Vazquez a Nazi patch that he wore during the mosque attack. She also allegedly agreed to "live stream the attacks planned that day, disseminate the recording publicly and then release the manifesto authored by the attackers purporting to justify the attack."

O'Neill said the livestream, which was transmitted via GoPro cameras attached to the helmets that Clark and Vazquez wore, was viewed by Santiago and two other people, which explains how investigators were able to zero in on her. Last week, he said, he conferred with Forsyth County Sheriff Bobby Kimbrough, other local law enforcement officials, the FBI, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Anand Ramaswamy about how to proceed with the case.

One question was whether to arrest Santiago right away or wait for an indictment.
O'Neill and the other officials decided an immediate arrest made sense because Santiago might pose an ongoing threat. "With the weekend approaching, holy days approaching," O'Neill said, "we didn't know what she was capable of."

Another question was whether to prosecute Santiago in state or federal court. If she were charged under federal law, O'Neill explained, "the time that she was looking at was only about three or four years." He may have been referring to the statute criminalizing "misprision of felony," which is punishable by up to three years in prison and consists of concealing and failing to report a federal felony. If Santiago were charged under state law with aiding and abetting the three murders in San Diego, by contrast, she would face a life sentence. O'Neill thought the latter option was more appropriate in light of "her part in this carnage."

If a defendant aids and abets a crime, North Carolina's model jury instruction explains, he "is guilty of the crime, just as if the defendant had personally done all the acts necessary to constitute that crime." Aiding and abetting requires three elements: 1) the crime was committed by another person, 2) the defendant knowingly "advised," "instigated," "encouraged," "procured," or "aided" the other person "to commit that crime," and 3) "the defendant's actions or statements caused or contributed to the commission of the crime."

To convict Santiago, prosecutors must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Santiago's role in livestreaming and recording the mosque attack, publishing the killers' manifesto, and supplying Vazquez with a Sonnenrad patch satisfies those three elements. That seems like a tall order, especially regarding the third element, which hinges on what might have happened if Clark and Vazquez had never communicated with Santiago. If they would have carried out their plan anyway, it is hard to see how Santiago's conduct "caused or contributed to" the murders they committed.

"When someone has credible knowledge of that a crime is gonna be planned or be committed, particularly any act of violence," FBI Special Agent in Charge Reid Davis said during the press conference, "the law requires them to come forward and report it. Failure to do so is not only irresponsible, but it can also be a crime." But that crime is a far cry from first-degree murder, and Santiago's alleged conduct, appalling as it is, does not seem to justify treating her as if she had personally shot and killed the victims of the mosque attack.

In defending that decision, O'Neill suggested that Santiago's real crime was participating in an online culture that radicalizes potentially violent young people. "There exists in our world an underground subculture," he said. "It's an echo chamber of intense hate against different cultures and religions." Participants in "this underground subculture of hate," he explained, "listen to each other" and "talk to each other" on "encoded platforms" like Signal, and "it radicalizes" them "to the point where they carry out these horrific crimes of violence and murder."

O'Neill urged parental awareness as one solution to that problem. But he also said "it is imperative" that "lawmakers prevent these sites" from "being accessible to young people." In response to a reporter's question, he reiterated that legislation was necessary, saying "we have the ability to stop people from glorifying their terroristic carnage for other people to watch." When asked whether there were plans to prosecute the two other people who watched the livestream of the mosque shooting, he declined to comment, saying "it's a continuing investigation."

O'Neill portrayed the charges against Santiago as part of a crackdown on "this subculture of hate," saying "maybe this is the precedent that we need moving forward." And in elaborating on that theme, he conflated the allegations of aiding and abetting murder with the expression of odious views.

Even people who had no foreknowledge of the mosque attack, O'Neill suggested, might face criminal charges simply for watching the livestream. He went further, arguing that the government should block access not only to such footage but also to websites that foment religious, racial, or ethnic animus, which are clearly protected by the First Amendment regardless of how hateful their content might be.

"Today we send a message, a strong message," Winston-Salem Police Chief William Penn said at the press conference. "If you commit a crime, especially a heinous crime, you will not be protected by a distance, you will not be protected by your computer monitor, and you will not be protected in your basement. You will be brought to justice."

Given O'Neill's broad description of the problem he is targeting, that "strong message" is rather alarming. Reasonable people can disagree about the appropriate charge or penalty for a 17-year-old who does what Santiago allegedly did. But her criminal culpability should hinge on the extent to which she encouraged or facilitated the crimes that Clark and Vazquez committed, as opposed to her opinions about Muslims, Jews, or black people. By presenting the case against her as part of a fight against "this subculture of hate," O'Neill blurs the distinction between crime and constitutionally protected speech.

title: California lawmakers pass bill allowing people to identify their Jewish ancestry on state forms
description: California would allow Jews to voluntarily identify their Jewish heritage on state forms under a bill the state Legislature passed Monday.  The bill, which lawmakers sent to Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk, ...
fullText:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California would allow Jews to voluntarily identify their Jewish heritage on state forms under a bill the state Legislature passed Monday.

The bill, which lawmakers sent to Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk, would require state agencies that collect demographic information to add "Jewish" as an option for ethnicity or ancestry. The goal is to give state officials and researchers better data on Jewish Californians, including their unemployment rates and representation in schools.

The data would enable lawmakers to create policies that address the needs of Jews in the state, said David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, an advocacy group.

"It's about inclusion as a community," Bocarsly said, noting the Legislature has passed laws in recent years to collect more inclusive demographic data on Middle Eastern, North African and LGBTQ+ communities.

Some opponents of the bill are worried about the idea of the state collecting such data given the traumatic history of the Nazi government keeping records of Jews during the Holocaust. The proposal would bar agencies from disclosing "personal identifying information," and bill author Henry Stern, a Democratic state senator who is Jewish, said California already has robust privacy protections that should assuage those concerns.

Sydney Levy of Jewish Voice for Peace, a progressive anti-Zionist group, wasn't convinced by that argument.

"When it comes to government holding lists of Jews, we do not trust your privacy guardrails," Levy said at a hearing on the bill.

Marc Dollinger, a Jewish studies professor at San Francisco State University, said in Jewish tradition, "Jews are not supposed to be counted."

"Ultimately, it becomes a question of trust: do California Jews have confidence that this form of data collection will support and protect them or will it elevate concerns over the possible harm this sort of counting can do?" he said in an email.

Since the bill would categorize Jewish identity as an ethnicity, it could help the state track hate crimes against Jews, Dollinger said.

Levy said he also disagrees with categorizing Jews as a single ethnic group.

"Latino Jews like myself, as well as other Jews of color, have cultures and experiences different from those of white Jews," Levy said at the hearing.

Under the bill, people could still identify their race in addition to selecting "Jewish" for their ethnicity. It would be similar to how some people identify as Latino ethnically while describing their race as white, Native American or Black. The legislation was updated Friday to exempt agencies from adding "Jewish" as an option on their forms if they would for some reason lose federal funding for making the change.

Stern started wearing a kippah to work in recent years, a sign of how his relationship to his Jewish identity has evolved throughout his life.

On the same day that Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023, which launched the war in Gaza, Stern was walking to synagogue with his daughter, pushing her in a stroller, when people in a car went out of their way to yell an antisemitic remark at them, he said.

Stern was wearing a kippah. He decided to wear it regularly after that.

Stern said it was a big shift for someone who wasn't very religious as a kid, though he would be reminded that he was different from other students in junior high school, when he was bullied for being Jewish. If Stern's bill had been in place back then, it would have been a way to ensure his identity was better represented, he said.

"This bill is just trying to create a little more space for those kinds of people — just let them be seen," Stern said. "I don't think it's going to be a radical transformation. I don't think it's going to change the world."

title: Newsom hit with lawsuit threat as whistleblower begs Trump for help with ‘monumental’ fraud scandal
description: Assemblyman Carl DeMaio says he plans to file a lawsuit against Gavin Newsom's new California law that he claims criminalizes citizen journalism.
fullText:
California's "monumental problem" with rampant fraud is about to get significantly worse, according to Republican state Assemblyman Carl DeMaio, after Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill that he warns will crack down on people investigating scammers.

Officially titled "Privacy for immigration support services providers," the new law creates privacy protections for immigration support service providers, employees and volunteers, including shielding their addresses and imposing penalties on those who publish their images on social media. DeMaio told Fox News Digital the bill amounts to criminalizing investigative journalism and works to "silence citizen journalists and shield taxpayer-funded organizations from public scrutiny."

"What does the Stop Nick Shirley Act do? It basically makes it illegal for a citizen journalist to document fraud of taxpayer money and post that on the internet in the form of an internet video," he said.

Newsom signed the bill into law last week, and it is set to take effect Oct. 1, 2027. DeMaio told Fox News Digital that he and a "coalition of civil liberty protectors" are prepared to file a lawsuit challenging the law.

Dems Ripped For 'Stop Nick Shirley Act' That Could 'Shield' Fraud And Abuse In California

"We have a plaintiff and are putting together the legal briefs," he said, adding, "It is a matter of time before we're going to get before a judge to stop this act."

"It is our hope," he continued, "that the U.S. Department of Justice will file to intervene in that case, because this is an open-and-shut infringement on our First Amendment rights."

DeMaio said California's fraud scandal makes the Minnesota fraud look like "garden variety government mismanagement."

"If you were worried about Somali daycare centers in Minnesota not having children in the daycare, take a look at California government NGOs receiving taxpayer funds and not having any sort of public services that they're delivering," he said. "They say they provide public services to immigrants when, in fact, they organize rallies, they harvest ballots, they endorse candidates and ballot measures during campaigns, and they are an extension of the Democrat Party."

DeMaio said the planned lawsuit follows discussions with the Justice Department's Office for Civil Rights.

Nick Shirley Warns California Bill Could Punish People Trying To Expose Government Fraud

"I have asked the U.S. Department of Justice Office of Civil Rights to look at the Stop Nick Shirley Act … to see if they can do anything to intervene to prevent the implementation of this law. We have been dialoguing with the Department of Justice, and now we have a game plan as to how we will proceed forward in the courts to overturn this unconstitutional law," he said.

Addressing Newsom directly, DeMaio said, "Gavin Newsom, once again, you're a bully trying to silence citizen watchdogs into not exercising their First Amendment rights and exposing your fraud, the billions of dollars that you've allowed to be wasted of precious taxpayer funds, all because you want the benefit of these left-wing NGOs to help you politically."

DeMaio said Newsom and California's Democratic supermajority "created such a monumental problem with fraud of taxpayer money being abused that it's clear that it is intentional."

"You're going to be exposed as a bully," he told Newsom. "You're going to be exposed as the fraud ringleader."

See It: La Dem Candidates Torched By Disgusted Residents After 'Disgraceful' Debate: 'Both Bad'

In response, Newsom spokesperson Diana Crofts-Pelayo told Fox News Digital that "this law has nothing to do with Nick Shirley" and that "the real controversy here is that MAGA Republicans are either lying to create up fake conspiracy theories, or none of them know how to read."

Crofts-Pelayo said the law does not affect Shirley's journalism, which Newsom's office previously referred to as "grifting" and "lying," and does not hide fraud.

Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of California Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón, both Democrats, for comment.

title: California mom has both legs amputated after suspected impaired driver plows into her restaurant lunch table
description: A California woman underwent three surgeries and a bilateral leg amputation after an alleged impaired driver crashed into a Boyle Heights restaurant.
fullText:
An elderly California mother had both her legs amputated after an alleged impaired driver crashed into the outdoor dining area of a restaurant where she was eating lunch.

Cristina Vargas, 81, was enjoying lunch at a sidewalk table outside Los Cinco Puntos in Los Angeles' Boyle Heights with her daughter, Gabriela Vargas, and their male friend when the SUV plowed into them at around 3:30 p.m. on July 7.

Surveillance footage obtained by KTLA shows an SUV veering onto the sidewalk and into the outdoor dining area.

Screeching tires were heard just before the SUV hit the group, sending patrons, the table and other items flying.

Arizona Grandpa To Undrgo Amputation After Collapsing On Scorching Sidewalk

"I remember I just heard screeching, and I was lifting up my head and I just saw headlights and a bumper and I heard a big boom," Gabriela told KTLA. "The next thing I knew, I was airborne."

Cristina's lower body was pinned under the vehicle and Gabriela suffered a head injury and a deep laceration on her knee. The two women and their male friend were rushed to a hospital for treatment.

Gabriela and the male friend have since recovered from their injuries, but Cristina's injuries were significantly worse, and she faces a long road to recovery.

Cristina underwent three surgeries and later had both of her legs amputated. She said she is thankful to be alive and has maintained a positive mindset.

She has been undergoing physical therapy at a rehabilitation center and will soon be allowed to go back home.

Cristina, a widowed mother of two, said she is looking forward to being surrounded by her family and friends.

"My goal is to give her the best quality of care from here on out," Gabriela said of her mother.

A police report alleges that the driver was impaired at the time of the crash. The unidentified woman was arrested and charged with multiple felonies, according to KTLA.

A GoFundMe created by a friend for the Vargas family has raised more than $30,000 as of Sunday night. The fundraiser said the family is facing massive medical bills, ongoing rehabilitation and daily living expenses.

"Cristina will need significant support to adapt to her new disability, including making their home accessible and covering the costs of specialized care. The road ahead is long and challenging, but with your help, they can focus on healing rather than the overwhelming financial stress," the fundraiser reads.

California Man Picks Up Explosive Device On A Beach During July 4 Cleanup, Loses Hand

The fundraiser described Cristina as a "vibrant and social person with a true lust for life."

"She loved to dance and was a regular at events at the senior center, bringing joy and energy wherever she went," the GoFundMe reads. "Her vivacious spirit and love for connecting with others made her a beloved member of the community. This sudden change is especially heartbreaking for someone who has always embraced life so fully and actively."

In an Aug. 17 update, Gabriela thanked supporters and said the recovery was progressing slowly.

"Thank you everybody for your love and support. We greatly appreciate it. It's a slow recovery but day by day we're getting through it. My mom's spirits remain hopeful as do mine. Recovery is very painful but she's giving it her all," Gabriela said.

title: Former California councilman's corruption unmasked after FBI finds cash buried in backyard
description: Ricardo Pacheco buried $62,900 in cash in his backyard as part of a bribery scheme involving Baldwin Park police union contracts and marijuana permits.
fullText:
A former California councilman who admitted burying nearly $63,000 in cash in his backyard was sentenced Friday to 18 months in federal prison for taking bribes tied to a police-union contract and commercial marijuana permits, prosecutors said.

Ricardo Pacheco, 63, spent more than two decades on the Baldwin Park City Council before resigning in 2020 as part of his plea deal. Federal prosecutors said he used his elected office to collect cash and funnel other payments through his church and political groups.

The Department of Justice said Pacheco and former Compton City Councilman Isaac Jacob Galvan carried out "corrupt acts while they were elected officials," including accepting and paying bribes for political support and city permits.

Hawaii's Democratic Lieutenant Governor Indicted In State Corruption Investigation

Pacheco was also fined $10,000 and ordered to forfeit $219,755. The FBI seized $83,145 in cash proceeds from him, including $62,900 that Pacheco said he had buried in two places in his backyard, prosecutors said. A restitution hearing is still to be scheduled.

Galvan, 39, received the same 18-month federal prison sentence and was ordered to pay $323,557 in restitution.

Former Gambino Associate Turned New Jersey Councilman Accused Of Running Loansharking Ring While In Office

The case began with the police-union deal.

Between January and October 2018, Pacheco solicited and received $37,900 from a Baldwin Park police officer in exchange for supporting the Baldwin Park Police Association's contract with the city, prosecutors said. The deal was worth at least $4.4 million over three years.

Massachusetts Mayor Charged With Wire Fraud In $1.5M Covid Relief Scheme

The officer was working at the FBI's direction after he and another officer approached the bureau to assist in its corruption investigation, according to the DOJ.

In October 2018, the officer handed Pacheco a $20,000 cash bribe inside an envelope at a Baldwin Park coffee shop, prosecutors said. Pacheco also directed $17,900 in checks to his church and political action committees that were set up in other people's names but controlled by him, according to the DOJ.

Maduro Ally Deported To Us Over Alleged Billion-dollar Corruption Scheme Tied To Oil, Food Program

Pacheco voted for the police association contract in March 2018.

Pacheco later became an FBI informant after agents caught him in a video-recorded sting at the coffee shop, according to the Los Angeles Times.

The outlet reported that Pacheco wore a concealed wire as investigators built cases that led to six indictments involving more than 20 people tied to local government and the marijuana industry.

The outlet also reported that the wider investigation implicated figures including Galvan, a former Baldwin Park city attorney, a Commerce city manager, a San Bernardino County planning commissioner and a marijuana distributor.

The case also uncovered an alleged pay-to-play system around marijuana permits in Baldwin Park.

Former California Mayor Admits To Secretly Working For China, Spreading Beijing Propaganda In Us

The city began allowing marijuana cultivation, manufacturing and distribution in 2017. Prosecutors said Pacheco soon began seeking money from businesses pursuing development agreements and related permits.

Galvan, who was then serving on the Compton City Council, offered consulting services to W&F International Corp., a Diamond Bar import-export business that wanted a marijuana permit in Baldwin Park, prosecutors said.

Galvan then helped facilitate $70,000 in bribes from the company's owner, Yichang Bai, to Pacheco in return for the councilman's votes and political backing, according to the DOJ.

Pacheco delivered, prosecutors said, voting in favor of W&F's permit in June and July 2018 and later supporting the company's effort to relocate its operations.

The payments were obscured through checks from third parties, including checks with blank payee lines, prosecutors said. When Pacheco later sought more money for his legal defense fund, Galvan told Bai the councilman wanted $25,000. Bai agreed to provide $20,000 through seven checks from bank accounts that were not his or W&F's, the DOJ said.

Galvan also admitted he failed to report about $560,525 in income to the IRS from 2017 through 2020. Prosecutors said the scheme caused a tax loss of $115,816.

Bai pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit bribery and was sentenced in July to 20 months in federal prison and a $3,000 fine.

title: Star student rejected by 16 colleges, hired by Google, gets legal win in racial discrimination suit
description: A Palo Alto, California, father declares victory after a judge denied the University of Washington's motion to dismiss their anti-Asian bias suit.
fullText:
A father in Palo Alto, California is declaring a victory in court after a federal judge allowed a civil rights lawsuit alleging anti-Asian bias in college admissions to move forward.

Nan Zhong and his son, Stanley Zhong, filed federal lawsuits against several elite institutions — including the University of California system, the University of Washington, the University of Michigan, and Cornell University. The complaints allege the universities engaged in "racially discriminatory admissions practices that disadvantage highly qualified Asian-American applicants."

One of their cases will now proceed in part against the University of Washington after a federal judge granted the university defendants' motion to dismiss in part and denied it in part.

title: Skarke rescues point for Union in six-goal thriller with Frankfurt
description: 1. FC Union Berlin opened its 2026/27 Bundesliga campaign on a sunny, 25-degree afternoon in the nation’s capital, hosting Eintracht Frankfurt at Stadion An der Alten Försterei.Union’s 2024/25 ca...
fullText:
1. FC Union Berlin opened its 2026/27 Bundesliga campaign on a sunny, 25-degree afternoon in the nation's capital, hosting Eintracht Frankfurt at Stadion An der Alten Försterei.

Union's 2024/25 campaign saw them under the leadership of Steffen Baumgart and history-making Marie-Louise Eta, moving up two places compared to their 2023/24 season from thirteenth to eleventh - with a 10-9-15 record and 35 points. Their Hessian opponents finished four places above them but could not balance Champions League football with their Bundesliga season, ultimately finishing one spot out of Europe in eighth with an 11-11-12 record and 44 points.

Union are undefeated in their last five matches against Frankfurt going into this meeting (3-2-0), having won their head-to-head matchup at home (4-3) and drawing away (1-1) last season. The last time Frankfurt won was in Berlin on 4. November 2023, a 3-0 result on goals from now-Manchester City FC forward Omar Marmoush (2', 14') and now-Feyenoord SC striker Nacho Ferri (82').

Union Berlin would see the first chance of the match in the second minute, as a cross into the right side of the box from Robin Koch was deflected away by the right leg of Marin Ljubičić for a corner. On the ensuing set piece, Josip Juranović's delivery into the centre of the box was met by a towering header from Ivorian international and new loan signing Emmanuel Latte Lath, above a leaping Noah Atubolu and top-centre to give the hosts the lead.

Ebnoutalib's brace, just 11 minutes into the match, became the third-fastest from a player on the first matchweek of the Bundesliga season - both Frank Mill (Borussia Mönchengladbach - FC Schalke 04, 1984/85) and Kevin Behrens (1. FC Union Berlin - 1. FSV Mainz 05) were able to do so in the first 9 minutes. At 50 seconds between goals, it was also one of the fastest braces in Bundesliga history since this data was counted, with FC Schalke 04's Edu having recorded a 47-second brace against 1. FC Nürnberg during the 2001/02 season.

Five minutes later, Eintracht Frankfurt would win a free kick on the left side of the ground, swung in by Keita Kosugi but cleared away by Rani Khedira. The ensuing corner would ultimately land in front of Younes Ebnoutalib, amidst a scramble at the goalmouth - and he smashed the ball past Matheo Raab and into the bottom-left corner to draw Die Adler level.

Ljubičić would restart play just seconds later, playing the ball back to Leopold Querfeld. The 22-year-old Austrian centre-back took a few seconds to evaluate his passing options, but it was a bit too much time - as Ebnoutalib came charging towards him and ultimately stripped him of possession. It led to a 1-on-1 between Ebnoutalib and Raab, with the former lifting the ball above the 27-year-old German goalkeeper. By the time that Zeno van den Bosch could run in to sweep the ball away, it already crossed the line - and the visitors jumped in front just seconds after finding their equaliser.

Frankfurt would continue to press in the minutes that followed, with Ebnoutalib searching for one of the fastest first half hat-tricks in Bundesliga history. In the eighteenth minute, Koch lobbed the ball into the centre of the box; Ebnoutalib and Can Uzun were both there, but the latter reached out to meet the ball, volleying it just above Raab and out of play for a goal kick to the hosts.

In the twenty-fourth minute, Kosugi would progress the ball for Frankfurt on the left side of the ground. Michel Aebischer lunged in for a harsh tackle and was almost instantly shown the first yellow card of the day by head official Bastian Dankert. The ensuing free kick was whipped in by Uzun, but landed right into the hands of Raab. Union would counter in the minutes that followed, as a pass from Latte Lath on the left side of the Frankfurt third ultimately landed in front of Ljubičić. His sliding chance to tap the ball bottom-right missed by a few metres, going out of play for a goal kick to the visitors.

Four minutes later, the match saw a rare delay, as while Frankfurt were passing the ball around in the centre of the ground, assistant referee René Rohde appeared to have picked up an injury on the sidelines. He abruptly went down the tunnel, with the other assistant official, Mitja Stegemann, relaying information to Dankert. After a six-minute delay, it was ultimately determined that fourth official Konrad Oldhafer would manage the offside flag on the right side of the ground, and that the match would continue with a drop ball.

Just before halftime, Ayoube Amaimouni would get a chance from distance to put Frankfurt into a two-goal advantage. It deflected off the arm of Querfeld - but not enough for Dankert to call a penalty to the visitors, given that the arm of the Austrian defender was close to his body at that moment. That would be the last notable play of the opening term, as the two sides would go into the locker rooms with Eintracht Frankfurt leading by two goals to one.

Shots in the first half finished 5-5, but the three goals were the only shots on target. Eintracht held 59% possession and had a 16% better pass accuracy - 78% on 175 completions, compared to 62% on 96 for Union.

Ljubičić kicked off the second half for the hosts - but after both sides consistently stopped each other in the midfield, it would be the visitors that would get the first chance of the term, albeit from distance. In the fifty-sixth minute, Farès Chaïbi would take a pass from Amaimouni to the centre of the Union half and then smashed a right-footed shot towards the bottom-right corner, not missing by much as it went past a standing Raab but off the side netting.

In the sixty-fifth minute, a long throw from Tim Rothe on the left side of the Eintracht half bounced off the ground, in front of substitute Tim Skarke, who came into the match for Latte Lath just four minutes earlier. The 29-year-old German attacking midfielder tried to half-volley the ball into the top-right corner, but mistimed his kick and the ball went off the back of his boot - directly into the hands of Atubolu.

Two minutes later, Eintracht would make sure that Union could not get .  Elias Baum took possession of the ball on the right side of the hosts' third after a failed clearance from Livan Burcu; his initial pass into the centre of the box, towards Ebnoutalib, was blocked by Burcu, and the rebound appeared to have gone off his arm, which was close to his body. The second attempt, a lob into the box, was successful, and within seconds, Ebnoutalib thundered it into the bottom-right corner to complete the hat-trick. The Union players were adamant that Baum touched it with his arm in an illegal manner, but it was quickly determined by the VAR officials that the contact was incidental - thus, under revised Bundesliga rules implemented in recent years, the goal stood.

Union would get a series of chances to pull the match back within one, none more notable than a cross into the box from Ljubičić that was met by a free header from Skarke in the seventy-fifth minute. Atubolu had a split-second to react to the ball heading towards the top-right corner, but leapt in time to glove it down with both hands.

Two minutes after that, Atubolu made a fine double save, denying a shot from distance towards the bottom-left corner from Rani Khedira, and then leaping to punch away a Josip Juranović shot towards the top-right corner with his left hand. Union would win a corner, cleared by Atubolu for another set piece; that one was quickly taken by Juranović and headed by Querfeld into the bottom-left corner to make the score 2-3.

Despite their best efforts, the hosts were unable to find an equaliser in the remaining ten minutes of the 90. Four minutes of stoppage time were added, Union quickly won a corner, and Juranović's cross was headed towards the bottom-left corner by Querfeld. Atubolu was ready to leap to deny it with both hands, but a deflection from Skarke with the right leg quickly caught him off-guard, tapped into the centre of the goal to send the Alte Försterei into delirium.

Neither side could get a late decider, but for Union, they remained unbeaten in their last six meetings against Frankfurt, with a 3-3 draw in an absolute thriller to open their 2026/27 Bundesliga campaign. Shots in the second half finished 14-7 to Union, 9-1 on target with 56% possession and a 74% accuracy on 151 passes to 72% on 123. Overall, shots finished 19-12 to Union, 10-3 on target with Frankfurt holding 52% possession; pass accuracy finished 75% on 298 passes for Frankfurt, 69% on 245 for Union.

1. FC Union Berlin will make a trip to Nordrhein-Westfalen to take on Bayer 04 Leverkusen in the second matchweek of the new season; that match is set for Saturday, 15.30 (CET). As for Eintracht Frankfurt, they will go back to the familiar Deutsche Bank Park to face FC Augsburg for the Sunday primetime match, with kickoff at 17.30 (CET).

title: Six government passport CAs that Python rejects and OpenSSL accepts
description: Parse an ICAO/BSI CSCA Master List (.ml) and export every Country Signing CA certificate — PEM bundle, TSV manifest, with an OpenSSL fallback for the certs strict ASN.1 parsers reject. - Eginn-33/c...
fullText:
Parse an ICAO / BSI CSCA Master List (.ml) and export every Country
Signing CA certificate inside it — as a PEM bundle, as a TSV manifest, or just
as a count.

One file, one dependency, no framework.

A Master List is the trust anchor set for electronic passports: to validate the
SOD on any eMRTD you need the issuing country's CSCA, and Master Lists are how
states distribute them in bulk. The format is specified in ICAO Doc 9303
Part 12 and BSI TR-03129:

That is not hard — but there is remarkably little public tooling that just
opens the file and gives you the certificates. Most eMRTD code buries the
parse inside a larger verification stack. This repo is the parse on its own.

Run against a real Master List with --strict and six entries drop on the
floor:

All six fail inside cryptography's Rust ASN.1 parser with:

They are not junk. OpenSSL reads every one of them:

These are live, government-issued CSCAs carrying trailing bytes in the
signature AlgorithmIdentifier that a strict DER parser rejects. Austria,
the UAE and Japan are not edge cases you get to skip — silently dropping them
means passports from those countries fail validation with a confusing
"unknown issuer" instead of a real error.

So the default path falls back to openssl x509 for anything cryptography
refuses, and the manifest records which parser produced each row:

Use --strict if you want the lenient path off and the failures visible.

openssl on PATH is optional; without it, --strict behaviour is the only
behaviour and the six certificates above are reported as unparsable.

With no output flags it prints statistics and exits — useful for diffing two
Master List releases.

See examples/manifest_sample.tsv for the
manifest shape.

No Master List is bundled here, and .gitignore refuses to commit one. Fetch
your own and keep it fresh: CSCAs roll over, and a stale trust store is how
you end up rejecting valid documents.

Neither of them will hand you the certificates out of a .ml file, which is
what this repo is for.

This tool reads public trust anchors — the certificates states publish
specifically so that anyone can validate the passports they issue. It handles
no private keys, no chip communication, and no passport data. It is the
boring, public half of eMRTD work, which is exactly why it can be open.

fullText:
Adam Mosseri is first top executive from Meta to testify in blockbuster lawsuit brought by 29 US states

Instagram’s CEO disputed allegations by US prosecutors that his company hid negative information from the public while testifying during a blockbuster social media trial.

“I am not trying to encourage my team to hide anything,” the CEO, Adam Mosseri, told a California courtroom on Tuesday.

Mosseri is the first top executive from Meta, which owns both Instagram and Facebook, to testify in a historic lawsuit brought by 29 US states. His testimony began toward the end of the day on Tuesday and is slated to continue on Wednesday.

When the executive was posed with multiple questions about not disclosing low user numbers for Instagram’s features geared toward teen safety, he brushed them aside, saying: “We don’t publish every single stat.”

Jason Slothouber, a prosecutor for the state of Colorado, asked specifically about a tool called Take a Break, meant to encourage teens to close Instagram if they’d been scrolling for a while. Slothouber pointed out that just 1.8% of teens signed up for the feature, and that while Mosseri had touted the tool, he never publicly disclosed that number.

“I’ve definitely said publicly that the opt-in rates are low,” Mosseri responded. “I don’t know if I’ve said numbers.”

The jury trial, taking place in federal court in Oakland, California, began with opening statements last week. The lawsuit centers on the states’ allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. The states additionally claim the social media company regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws.

If found liable, Meta could be forced to pay damages as high as $200bn and change the design of its products to make them safer for kids. Legal experts say the outcome of this trial could fundamentally change the way social media apps function for young people.

Meta has denied all allegations, saying the states are chasing an “outlandish payout”. A spokesperson said Tuesday that Meta’s safety teams strive to be industry-leading and that Mosseri’s testimony showed the company does research to find ways to improve user experience.

Mosseri became the head of Instagram in 2018 and over the years has faced scrutiny about whether he may have dismissed internal warnings about the platform’s addictive design and negative effects on young people. He was called to testify before a Senate committee in December 2021 and as a witness in other trials about the alleged harm of social media to children.

On Tuesday, Slothouber asked Mosseri about a blog post he had published just one day before his Senate testimony. The post was titled “raising the standard for protecting teens and supporting parents online” and included the announcement of the Take a Break tool. Slothouber questioned Mosseri about the timing of his post.

“We had made progress, and we wanted to get the progress out, so we could talk about the progress,” Mosseri responded.

Slothouber then asked the CEO whether he was aware of the phrase “drumbeat messaging”, the idea of saying something repeatedly until it’s drummed into people’s heads. Mosseri said he had and that it’s necessary when dealing with parents and safety features. “We need to repeat it to raise awareness of those tools,” Mosseri testified.

Over the last week, jurors also heard from Arturo Béjar, a former Meta safety engineer turned whistleblower, who testified that the company has a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its platforms. They also heard from a psychologist and other former and current company employees.

The trial is expected to last through September with several other witnesses, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

fullText:
US tech giant agrees to establish further protections for teens such as daily usage limits and blocks on nighttime use

Meta agreed to significant changes to its Instagram and Facebook apps in a settlement that ended a landmark lawsuit on Wednesday. Dozens of US states had accused the tech giant of addicting and harming children with dangerous products.

The agreement curtails a major trial in California and will require the social media company to pay up to $17bn. Meta agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, including daily usage limits and blocks on nighttime use nationwide in the US.

This is the first time in the US that Meta has been forced to change key features of the experience of everyday users.

The jury trial, which took place in federal court in Oakland, California, began with opening statements just last week. California and 28 other US states sued the $1.36tn (£1tn) company over allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. The states additionally claimed the social media company regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws. As part of the settlement, the company denies wrongdoing.

“Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of a difference for children and their families,” Rob Bonta, the attorney general for California, said in a statement. “Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms – and will do it within months.”

Bonta said those changes included time limits, stopping notifications during school, a block on the app during critical overnight hours, bans on plastic surgery filters and more.

The $17bn settlement will be divided between the states over a period of 10 years, subject to court approval. For example, California would receive between $1.5bn and $2.1bn and Colorado will get about $615m.

“The relief we are getting in this settlement is very meaningful and well beyond what any court has ordered or is likely to order,” said Phil Weiser, the attorney general for Colorado, adding: “The focus of this case was to protect our kids.”

Throughout the proceedings, Meta denied all allegations saying states are chasing an “outlandish payout”. On Wednesday, the company’s chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, said the settlement reached with the states would only work if all social media companies changed their platform designs.

“Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok, Snap, and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away,” Mahoney said in a statement. “As a parent, I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically, and of this new groundbreaking agreement. But its success depends on all other social media platforms following Meta’s lead.”

Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap face thousands more similar US lawsuits brought by families, individuals, school districts and other attorneys general. Meta and YouTube lost the first of those cases to go to trial in February, being ordered to pay $6m to the young woman who brought the suit. (TikTok and Snap settled before the case went to trial.) Two more lawsuits that were slated to go to trial this summer, one federal and one in California state court, also settled for undisclosed sums.

Meta lost a separate suit, brought by the attorney general of New Mexico, where it was ordered to pay nearly $1bn to the state of New Mexico for allowing child sexual exploitation on its platforms.

The trial in Oakland was expected to last for several weeks with dozens of witnesses taking the stand. Instead, there were only four days of proceedings.

Jurors first heard from the states’ star witness, Arturo Béjar, a former Meta safety engineer turned whistleblower. He testified that the company had a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its platforms.

Béjar said that Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s CEO, was aware of the harms of Instagram and Facebook, but that the executive publicly touted the platforms’ safety.

“I felt that he created a false and misleading impression of Facebook’s commitment to young people,” Béjar testified.

Zuckerberg had been listed as a witness in the trial but did not testify before the settlement agreement was reached.

On Tuesday, questioning of Adam Mosseri, the Instagram CEO, began with the lawyer for the states accusing the company of touting safety features for teens, but not being forthcoming that young people don’t use them.

When the executive was faced with multiple questions about not disclosing those low user numbers, Mosseri brushed them aside, saying: “We don’t publish every single stat.”

title: Utilities Break California Lobbying Record Under Newsom While Former Aides Lead
description: New disclosures show utilities spent a record $16.7 million lobbying Sacramento through the first six quarters of the 2025–2026 legislative session as…
fullText:
New disclosures show utilities spent a record $16.7 million lobbying Sacramento through the first six quarters of the 2025–2026 legislative session as lawmakers consider a utility bailout in end of session scramble

Sacramento, CA— California’s three largest investor-owned utilities — Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E), Southern California Edison (Edison), and Sempra Energy (Sempra) — have already mounted the most expensive lobbying campaign in state history, spending $16.7 million lobbying Governor Gavin Newsom’s administration, the Legislature and state regulators through the first six reporting quarters of the 2025–2026 legislative session, according to new disclosures released today.

Consumer Watchdog’s review of CAL-ACCESS lobbying records dating back to the 1999–2000 legislative sessionfound the current session has already surpassed every previous utility lobbying campaign on record — even though two quarterly reporting periods remain before the session concludes.

At the same time, utilities have increasingly declined to answer reporters’ questions directly, instead referring media inquiries to Wildfire Victims First, a new disinformation coalition funded entirely by California’s investor-owned utilities and utility political committees. Despite its name, the organization is not funded by independent wildfire survivor groups but instead is pushing a utility bailout in an end of session scramble. The coalition’s spokesman, Nathan Click, previously served as Governor Gavin Newsom’s communications director and chief spokesman before founding the Sacramento communications firm now representing the organization. Consumer Watchdog also found that Wildfire Victims First’s television advertising is being placed by Polaris Campaign Media, the affiliated media-buying firm of Bearstar Strategies, Governor Newsom’s longtime political consulting firm.

Utilities spent more than $4.35 million lobbying Sacramento during the second quarter of 2026 alone, including more than $353,000 lobbying the California Public Utilities Commission. PG&E accounted for nearly three-quarters of all utility lobbying reported during the quarter, spending nearly $3.2 million.

Through the first six reporting quarters of the 2025–2026 legislative session, PG&E, Edison and Sempra have spent a combined $16.7 million lobbying state government, including $15.9 million on general lobbying and more than $870,000 lobbying the California Public Utilities Commission.

Consumer Watchdog’s review of lobbying disclosures since Governor Gavin Newsom took office shows utility lobbying has climbed dramatically during his administration. The previous high-water mark came during the 2023–2024 legislative session, when utilities spent $16.1 million lobbying Sacramento. With two quarterly reporting periods still remaining, the 2025–2026 session has already surpassed that total, making it the most expensive utility lobbying campaign and under the Newsom administration.

The record-breaking lobbying campaign comes during one of the most consequential legislative sessions for California’s investor-owned utilities in years, as lawmakers and regulators decide who ultimately pays the costs of catastrophic wildfires:

“Utilities aren’t just spending record amounts lobbying Sacramento,” said Carmen Balber, Executive Director of Consumer Watchdog. “This is the largest utility lobbying campaign in modern California history, unfolding as Governor Newsom considers another end-of-session utility bailout. While utilities marshal lobbyists, political consultants and public relations campaigns, wildfire survivors are fighting to preserve their legal rights. That’s the worst of California politics.”

“They burned down our homes. Now they’re spending millions pretending to be wildfire survivors while real survivors fight to get home. Together with millions of Americans, we call on Governor Newsom to stop bailing out utility monopolies and start protecting the people they harmed,” said Joy Chen, founder of Every Fire Survivor’s Network.

Every Fire Survivor’s Network and Consumer Watchdog are leading the No Utility Bailouts campaign at DearNewsom.org, a coalition of public officials and organizations representing more than 3.5 million Americansurging Governor Newsom to reject another utility bailout.

The dual lobbying and communications strategy reflect the extraordinary political stakes surrounding California’s wildfire and insurance crisis, where Governor Newsom has emerged as the central decision-maker. With a new legislative bailout language expected this month, the outcome of those debates could determine who ultimately bears the cost of California’s next catastrophic wildfire — utility shareholders, taxpayers, ratepayers or survivors themselves.

“When utilities are simultaneously mounting the most expensive lobbying campaign in California history while Governor Newsom’s former chief spokesman serves as the face of their utility-funded coalition and his longtime political consulting network helps promote its message, Californians have every reason to ask whether utility influence has become too deeply embedded in the state’s decision-making. Wildfire survivors deserve transparency, accountability and confidence that these decisions are being made in the public interest, not the utilities’.”

title: California dad paralyzed from neck down after diving into ocean to rescue child

fullText:
A California father of five was paralyzed from the neck down after entering the ocean in an effort to help a young child who his family said was caught in a rip current.

Josh Collette, 42, was spending time with his family at Riviera Beach in San Clemente, California, on Aug. 15, when a child believed to be 7- or 8-years-old became caught in a rip current, the man's sister, Hillary Collette, told KTLA.

title: This Silicon Valley campus was a paradise. Bulldoze it
description: A developer’s plan for 665 apartments at Sunset magazine’s HQ has angered locals. I ran the magazine — and think California needs housing more than a shrine to suburbia.
fullText:
A developer’s plan for 665 apartments at Sunset magazine’s HQ has angered locals. I ran the magazine — and think California needs housing more than a shrine to suburbia.

My first glimpse of the Sunset magazine campus in Menlo Park was late on a February afternoon in 2013. I had just flown in from gray-slush-covered New York City, and while I knew California from attending Cal and living in San Francisco for a decade, this was another world.

Huge wooden doors opened to red-tiled floors, beamed ceilings, Spanish colonial antiques, shaded terraces, and a close-cropped lawn centered on an ancient live oak. A garden ran along a creek north to south — a microcosm of the West Coast, from redwoods and azalea at one end to cacti and succulents at the other. “It’s as if Don Draper designed a mission,” my husband marveled. I was enchanted. Within a month, I was walking Sunset’s halls and garden paths daily as editor-in-chief, reveling in my luck.

Of course, you had to overlook the warning signs. The rats that had taken up residence in the walls. The frayed carpets. And the empty building across the street, with its dead fountain and chipped tiles, once home to the books and CD-ROM (remember those?) division of the company, disbanded after Time Inc. bought Sunset Publishing from the Lane family in 1990. The C-suite honchos had long ago shipped much of the wine in our cellar off to their offices in New York City. No money was going in; only out.

I’d been through enough corporate downsizings to know where things were headed. I still have a stack of PowerPoints with arguments for how to expand Sunset, including new uses for the depopulated campus (startup lab? community space? sell half for townhouses?). By the time the company announced that it was cashing in on the real estate (reported sale price: at least $77 million (opens in new tab)) and moving us to cheaper offices in Oakland, I knew my time was up too.

That was 11 years ago. The developer who now owns the property at 80 Willow Road is planning to build a massive skyscraper complex (opens in new tab): retail and office space, a school, a hotel, and 665 apartments, 100 of them affordable. The proposal goes a long way toward addressing the state-mandated housing allotment of nearly 3,000 units for Menlo Park by 2030, but it has been fought by locals at every turn over its environmental impact and scale — a fight likely to continue, despite Attorney General Rob Bonta’s recent slap at Menlo Park (opens in new tab) for its alleged attempts to stall the approval process.

It’s still possible that the city and the developer can negotiate a scaled-back project for the historic site, avoiding ruinous litigation on both sides. But the precise scale of the project matters less than the fact that something dramatically different — and bigger — should go there. The dream of idyllic suburban life that Sunset’s building represents is dead, dead, dead — unsustainable and unaffordable for all but the very few. Why hang on?

Think about the history of our region: When the Sunset campus was built, ranch houses were supplanting fruit orchards up and down the valley at a furious clip: More than 5,000 homes were built in Menlo Park alone between 1950 and 1960. These dwellings were simple, similar, cheap, and far from chic. Malvina Reynolds’ famous song called this suburban growth “little boxes on the hillside … all made out of ticky-tacky.” She thought the people who lived in them were ticky-tacky too.

But the burgeoning post-war middle class flocking to those houses was Sunset’s audience. Founded in 1898 by the Southern Pacific Railroad to inspire travelers and buyers for its land (you can still take a ride on the Sunset Limited line), Sunset under the Lane family became an essential guide to Western living for newcomers encountering their first artichoke. The Lanes followed their readers from San Francisco to Menlo Park in 1951, commissioning Clifford May, the “father of the ranch house,” to design its new headquarters as a working laboratory. Our test kitchen was a suburban-style kitchen, not something only a chef could use. Our test gardens yielded endless lessons in how to zhuzh up your backyard, how to grill tri-tip, how to build a redwood planter, where to go car camping, how to make tamale pie, how to put a deck around your hot tub — the magazine inspired people in suburban California and well beyond to embrace it all.

Forty years later, the assumptions underlying that lifestyle — cheap gas, plentiful housing — had gone up in carbon-emitting smoke. As new construction slowed to a trickle, and average home prices rocketed into the millions, Sunset employees could no longer be expected to live within 10 miles of the office. The guy who helped me open an account at the local Wells Fargo told us he lived 90 minutes away; his parents had lost their Menlo Park house in the 2008 crash, and for a time he lived in his car. My husband, desperate for diversion (and diversity) after a year of walking our elderly dog through the silent streets of Los Altos, finally convinced me to move north to San Francisco. In my last summer as editor, I rented a $900-per-month studio with a single bed in a converted garage near the office so I could avoid 101 traffic at least a couple of days a week.

Most of the Sunset staff were enduring commutes more soul-sucking than mine. Still, leaving that peaceful bubble of a building was painful. I talked up the move to our new office in Oakland as a natural evolution: Our job was to reflect our readers’ lives; now they were back in the cities. Our most popular garden stories were about planting vegetables in containers; readers wanted more stories on home decorating for small spaces. We had always attuned ourselves to how the West was changing and what we needed to do to adapt. Magazines aren’t museums.

I share the nostalgia for that magical building, those enchanting gardens. But how can we afford to indulge in nostalgia when the housing crisis is so acute? The state estimates that we’ll need 2.5 million housing units by 2030, a million of them low-income. Why should Menlo Park get a pass? Big developments in California always seem to bring out the “But it will be like Manhattan!” argument. (I always think, well, at least Manhattan is fun.) Surely, in this land of innovation, we can come up with another example to guide us. I choose to live half my life in Paris — double the density of San Francisco but human-scale (opens in new tab) even so, designed for walking, dotted with parks and ever-more pedestrianized streets, neighborhoods served by a network of metro trains that come every two minutes. Closer to home, Pittsburgh and Chicago are dense yet eminently livable, with single-family houses interspersed with large apartment complexes and even skyscrapers.

Years of missed opportunities and narrow thinking have brought us here — to the land of low-slung suburban houses that only one-percenters can afford (and that are often torn down to make way for grander structures). There would be no reason to build 665 apartments in one shot if Menlo Park (and every California city) had embraced more sensible development over the last several decades — relaxing rules for parking, modernizing construction codes, speeding up approvals, encouraging building apartments over every storefront (yes, like Paris). The state’s 2022 housing law (opens in new tab) is designed to make it easier to incorporate housing into commercially zoned property like the 80 Willow site. We need that law. Because local control has failed us — keeping us focused on our own beautiful backyards while blind to the needs of others. Some of my ex-colleagues are praying that a sympathetic tech overlord will swoop in to buy out the developer and maintain the idyllic campus we once enjoyed. I can’t help but think of Marie Antoinette and her cute little sheep barn at Versailles.

Sunset, amid its travel itineraries, garden plans, and recipes, always also managed to pose big questions: How do we live well together on this trembling edge of the continent? How can we do so without disenfranchising our children and ruining the beauty we have inherited?

Maybe the best way to pay homage to Sunset’s history is to face reality: Tear down the building and start over.

Peggy Northrop was editor-in-chief of Sunset magazine from 2013 to 2015, when it won its first-ever National Magazine Award for general excellence.
